prompt: Why do pulses in typical solid-glass telecommunications fibre propagate at about two-thirds of the speed of light (c)?

options.text: Because light bounces from side to side, so it travels a longer zig-zag path
options.explanation: A geometrical zig-zag explanation is not sufficient, especially for a single spatial mode. Pulse velocity depends on the effective group index.

options.text: Its effective group index is about 1.47, so pulses travel at about the speed of light divided by 1.47
options.explanation: Correct. The group index incorporates the relevant propagation/dispersion behaviour; the speed of light divided by 1.47 is about 0.68 of the speed of light.

options.text: Because the optical amplifiers along the route add delay
options.explanation: Amplifiers (EDFAs) add a tiny amount of delay, but the two-thirds figure applies over any length of glass, including a short patch cable with no amplifier.

options.text: Because the electrons in the fibre move slowly
options.explanation: There are no conduction electrons carrying the signal in fibre; it's light. (And in copper, electron drift speed isn't the signal speed either.)

workedExample:
Using the rounded group index 1.47:

```formula
v_group = c / n_group
v_group ≈ (3 × 10⁸ m/s) / 1.47
v_group ≈ 2.04 × 10⁸ m/s
t_km = 1000 m / v_group ≈ 4.9 µs
where
v_group: the speed at which a pulse travels along the fibre, in metres per second (m/s)
c: the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s
n_group: the fibre's effective group index, about 1.47 (no unit)
t_km: the time a pulse takes to cross one kilometre (1000 metres)
m: metres
s: seconds
µs: microseconds, millionths of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: pulses travel at about 0.68 of the speed of light, so each kilometre of fibre takes about 4.9 µs.
```

Use a fibre/wavelength-specific group index for precision; single mode does not mean a literal straight ray.

prompt: For a direct standard 10 Gbit/s link over a 2 km cable route, compare Cat6a/10GBASE-T, OM4/10GBASE-SR and single-mode/10GBASE-LR, without intermediate repeaters. Which listed pairing has the specified reach, assuming a compliant optical loss budget?

options.explanation: 10GBASE-T is limited to 100 m. 2 km is twenty times too far without repeaters.
10GBASE-SR over compliant OM4 supports 400 m, below this 2 km requirement.
Correct for the specified 10GBASE-LR equipment and compliant single-mode channel, rated up to 10 km. Connector/splice loss and compatibility still matter.
Coax works for cable TV broadband, but 10 Gbit/s Ethernet over 2 km of coax isn't a standard option, and attenuation at those frequencies would be severe.

workedExample: For these specified pairings, Cat6a/10GBASE-T supports up to 100 m, OM4/10GBASE-SR up to 400 m, and single-mode/10GBASE-LR up to 10 km. Choose the last for the 2 km route after checking equipment compatibility and optical loss budget; fibre type alone does not specify reach.

prompt: A 120 km span of single-mode fibre loses 0.2 dB per km. Roughly what fraction of the launched optical power reaches the far end?

options.explanation: This treats 24 dB as a 24% loss. Decibels are logarithmic: every 10 dB is a factor of 10.
About 4% of the power is what 14 dB of loss leaves. Recheck the total: 120 × 0.2 = 24 dB.
Correct. Total loss is 24 dB: 20 dB is a factor of 100 and the other 4 dB a factor of about 2.5, so about 1/250 of the power arrives.
24 dB of loss leaves a fraction of about 0.00398, or 0.398%. This distractor is three orders of magnitude too small.

workedExample:
```formula
A = αd
A = 0.2 dB/km × 120 km = 24 dB
P_out / P_in = 10^(−A / 10)
P_out / P_in = 10^(−2.4)
P_out / P_in = 10^(−2) × 10^(−0.4)
P_out / P_in ≈ 0.01 × 0.4 = 0.004
where
A: the total loss over the span, in decibels (dB)
α: alpha, the loss per kilometre, 0.2 dB/km
d: the span length, 120 kilometres (km)
dB: decibels: every 10 dB of loss divides the power by 10
km: kilometres
P_out: the optical power reaching the far end
P_in: the optical power launched into the fibre
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 24 dB of loss divides the power by about 250, so only about **0.4%** of the launched light arrives.
```

This accounts only for the stated distributed loss. Whether the link works requires receiver sensitivity, launch power, connector/splice losses, dispersion and any amplification; no universal amplifier spacing is implied.

prompt: Two trading sites are 1,200 km apart in a straight line. The best fibre route is 1,300 km long. A microwave tower chain follows nearly the straight line. Roughly how much one-way latency does microwave save, counting propagation only? Use 204,000 km/s in glass and 300,000 km/s in air as the specified approximations.

options.explanation: This underestimates badly. Even the extra 100 km of fibre alone costs about 0.5 ms, and the larger effect is the speed difference between glass and air.
This compares 1,200 km at c (4.0 ms) with 1,200 km in fibre (5.9 ms), ignoring that the fibre route is 100 km longer.
Correct. Fibre: 1,300 km at ~204,000 km/s ≈ 6.4 ms. Microwave: 1,200 km at ~300,000 km/s = 4.0 ms. Saving ≈ 2.4 ms.

options.text: Nothing; both carry data at the speed of light
options.explanation: The question specifies a slower propagation speed in glass and an air speed close to c. Those assumptions, together with route length, determine the calculated delay.

workedExample:
Propagation delay is distance divided by speed, on each route:

```formula
t_fibre = d_fibre / v_fibre
t_fibre = 1,300 km / (204,000 km/s)
t_fibre ≈ 6.37 ms
t_air = d_air / v_air
t_air = 1,200 km / (300,000 km/s)
t_air = 4.00 ms
Δt = t_fibre − t_air ≈ 2.4 ms
where
t_fibre: the one-way propagation time over the fibre route
d_fibre: the fibre route length, 1,300 kilometres (km)
v_fibre: the signal speed in glass, about 204,000 km/s (the speed of light divided by 1.47)
t_air: the one-way propagation time over the microwave route
d_air: the microwave route length, 1,200 km
v_air: the signal speed in air, about 300,000 km/s
Δt: delta t, the time saved by the microwave route
km: kilometres; km/s is kilometres per second
s: seconds
ms: milliseconds, thousandths of a second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: the microwave path is both shorter and about 1.47 times faster, saving about **2.4 ms** one-way, about 37% of the fibre time.
```

The calculation excludes equipment and retransmission delay. Capacity and weather availability depend on frequency, route, antennas and engineering; the calculation alone establishes neither.
